  • Inverting IRIS Observations with MART

Inverting IRIS Observations with MART#

The main target of ESIS-I is the \(\text{O\,V}\;630\,\AA\) spectral line. To our knowledge, high-quality spectroheliograms of this line are not available to use as a test dataset. The Coronal Diagnostic Spectrometer (CDS) [Harrison et al., 1996] and the Solar Ultraviolet Measurements of Emitted Radiation (SUMER) [Wilhelm et al., 1995] have both observed this line, but their spatial or spectral resolution is not sufficient to use as a test for ESIS (but see Landi et al. [2000] for a possible SUMER candidate). Instead, we will use observations of the \(\text{Si\,IV}\;1394\,\AA\) spectral line from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS) [De Pontieu et al., 2014] as a proxy for the \(\text{O\,V}\;630\,\AA\) line. These observations will be imaged through a linearized model of the ESIS-I optics to create synthetic ESIS images. We will then use MART to invert these images and test how well it recovers the original scene.

[1]:

import IPython.display
import dataclasses
import warnings
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.colors
import astropy.units as u
import astropy.visualization
import named_arrays as na
import ctis
import esis

Loading the Test Scene#

Load an IRIS observation to use as a test scene to invert, with esis.flights.f1.data.synth.scene_iris(). This function shifts and scales the \(\text{Si\,IV}\;1394\,\AA\) spectral line observed by IRIS to match the \(\text{O\,V}\;630\,\AA\) line observed by ESIS, and keeps only the part of the spectrum within velocity_max of line center. The first time it is called, it downloads the IRIS raster.

[2]:

velocity_max = 250 * u.km / u.s

[3]:

%%time
scene = esis.flights.f1.data.synth.scene_iris(
    time_start="2014-07-04 11:40",
    velocity_max=velocity_max,
)

Subtract the average helioprojective \(x\) and \(y\) coordinates from the scene to place the observation at disk center.

[4]:

scene.inputs.position = scene.inputs.position - scene.inputs.position.mean()

Select the first raster of the observation to invert. The scene is already a radiance, so the mean exposure time of the raster steps can stand for all of them.

[5]:

scene = scene[{scene.axis_time: 0}]
scene.timedelta = scene.timedelta[{scene.axis_time: 0}].mean(scene.axis_detector_x)

With its default scaling, the ratio of the quiet-Sun radiances of the two lines, this scene is about three times as bright as an average active region in \(\text{O\,V}\;630\,\AA\). Rescale it so that its mean radiance is the average radiance of an active region measured by Vernazza and Reeves [1978], esis.flights.f1.spectrum.O_V.radiance_active_region. This is the same as multiplying the radiance_scale of scene_iris() by this factor.

[6]:

dw = scene.inputs.wavelength.volume_cell(scene.axis_wavelength)
radiance = (scene.outputs * dw).sum(scene.axis_wavelength)
scale = esis.flights.f1.spectrum.O_V.radiance_active_region / radiance.mean()
scale = scale.to(u.dimensionless_unscaled)
scene.outputs = scene.outputs * scale
scale

Defining a Model of the ESIS Instrument#

We use the optical design of the first flight of ESIS, esis.flights.f1.optics.design().

[10]:

design = esis.flights.f1.optics.design()

Raytracing every cell of the scene would be too slow to use in an inversion, so we linearize the design instead, with linearize(). This traces one set of rays and fits a distortion model, a vignetting model, and an effective area model to them. The result is a LinearSystem, which images a scene by regridding it onto the sensors instead of raytracing it. Here we sample the system at 11 wavelengths across the passband of the instrument.

[11]:

design.wavelength = na.linspace(
    start=design.wavelength_min.mean(),
    stop=design.wavelength_max.mean(),
    axis="fit-wavelength",
    num=11,
)

[12]:

%%time
system_linear = design.system.linearize()

CPU times: user 3.7 s, sys: 208 ms, total: 3.91 s
Wall time: 1.92 s

Save the name of the logical axis representing the four channels of ESIS, and a label for each channel.

[13]:

axis_channel = design.axis_channel
channel = "Channel " + design.camera.channel.astype(str)

Creating Synthetic ESIS Images#

Each synthetic image is one exposure of the cameras of the design, which lasts timedelta_exposure.

[14]:

design.camera.timedelta_exposure

[14]:
$10 \; \mathrm{s}$

To calculate synthetic images, apply the image() method of the linearized system to the IRIS scene. This step includes the photon shot noise and the read noise of the sensors.

The weights that map the scene onto the sensors take about 2.2 GB of memory per velocity bin, so chunk_size=8 images 8 velocity bins at a time and adds up the results. With this setting the cell below needs about 20 GB of memory, so lower chunk_size on a machine with less.

[15]:

%%time
images = system_linear.image(scene, chunk_size=8)

CPU times: user 2min 16s, sys: 14.5 s, total: 2min 31s
Wall time: 49.3 s

MART needs images that are not negative, so set any pixel that the read noise pushed below zero to zero.

[16]:

images = np.maximum(images, 0)

Display the central part of all four synthetic images.

Defining the Grid of the Reconstruction#

IRIS resolves the Sun more finely than ESIS, both in space and in wavelength. ESIS cannot recover structure smaller than its own pixels, so we reconstruct the scene on a coarser grid, with one ESIS pixel per cell in each direction.

dispersion_doppler() measures the Doppler velocity interval imaged onto one pixel from a raytrace, here at the rest wavelength of the line. It is the same for every channel, so take the mean over the channels.

[18]:

dispersion = design.dispersion_doppler(wavelength_rest).mean(axis_channel)
dispersion

[18]:

ScalarArray(
    ndarray=17.46165202 km / (pix s),
    shape={},
)

plate_scale() measures the angle imaged onto one pixel along each axis of the sensor. The grating magnifies the image along the dispersion, the \(x\) axis of the sensor, so a pixel spans a smaller angle along it than across it. The channels disperse in different directions on the sky, so we use the plate scale across the dispersion, the larger of the two, for both axes of the grid.

[19]:

plate_scale = design.system.plate_scale(wavelength_rest).y.mean(axis_channel)
plate_scale = plate_scale.to(u.arcsec / u.pix)
plate_scale

[19]:

ScalarArray(
    ndarray=0.77020829 arcsec / pix,
    shape={},
)

Use the dispersion and the plate scale as the steps of the new grid, built with ctis.arange(), which covers the same velocities and the same field of view as the IRIS scene.

[20]:

velocity_degraded = ctis.arange(
    start=-velocity_max,
    stop=+velocity_max,
    step=dispersion * u.pix,
    axis=scene.axis_wavelength,
)

[21]:

position_degraded = ctis.arange(
    start=scene.inputs.position.min(),
    stop=scene.inputs.position.max(),
    step=plate_scale * u.pix,
    axis=na.Cartesian2dVectorArray(
        x=scene.axis_detector_x,
        y=scene.axis_detector_y,
    )
)

[22]:

coordinates_degraded = na.TemporalDopplerPositionalVectorArray.from_velocity(
    time=scene.inputs.time.mean(scene.axis_detector_x),
    velocity=velocity_degraded,
    wavelength_rest=wavelength_rest,
    position=position_degraded,
)

Regrid the IRIS scene onto the coarser grid with ctis.regrid(). This degraded scene is the ground truth that we compare the inversion against.

[23]:

scene_degraded = ctis.regrid(
    coordinates_input=scene.inputs,
    coordinates_output=coordinates_degraded,
    values_input=scene.outputs,
    axis_wavelength=scene.axis_wavelength,
    axis_position=(scene.axis_detector_x, scene.axis_detector_y),
)
scene_degraded = scene.replace(
    inputs=coordinates_degraded,
    outputs=scene_degraded,
)

[24]:

scene_degraded.show();

Inverting the Synthetic ESIS Images#

Now for the tricky part, inverting these images into a reconstructed scene using MART.

To do this, wrap the linearized system in a ctis.instruments.OptikaInstrument, which images and backprojects scenes defined on the coarser grid.

[25]:

instrument = ctis.instruments.OptikaInstrument(
    system=system_linear,
    coordinates_scene=coordinates_degraded,
    channel=design.camera.channel,
    axis_channel=design.axis_channel,
    axis_wavelength=scene.axis_wavelength,
    axis_scene_xy=(scene.axis_detector_x, scene.axis_detector_y),
)

An important part of using MART effectively is the initial guess supplied to the algorithm. Here, the guess is the product of a spatial component and a spectral component.

The spatial component is the “poor man’s zeroth order image”, which is found by backprojecting each ESIS image onto the sky, with backproject(), and then taking the minimum along the channel axis. A feature that is smeared along the dispersion direction of one channel is smeared in a different direction in the others, so the minimum suppresses the smearing. To backproject onto the sky without spreading the light in wavelength, use a copy of the instrument with only one wavelength bin, the one that the images are integrated over.

[26]:

instrument_monochromatic = dataclasses.replace(
    instrument,
    coordinates_scene=coordinates_degraded.replace(wavelength=images.inputs.wavelength),
)

[27]:

%%time
backprojected_monochromatic = instrument_monochromatic.backproject(images, unit=scene.outputs.unit)

CPU times: user 4.79 s, sys: 174 ms, total: 4.97 s
Wall time: 4.28 s

[28]:

min_monochromatic = np.min(backprojected_monochromatic, axis=axis_channel)[{axis_channel: 0}]

Plot the spatial component of the guess.

with astropy.visualization.quantity_support():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(constrained_layout=True)
    img = na.plt.pcolormesh(

        min_monochromatic.inputs.position.y,
        C=min_monochromatic.outputs.mean(axis_wavelength).value,

        ax=ax,

    )

[30]:

guess_spatial = min_monochromatic.outputs
guess_spatial = guess_spatial / guess_spatial.sum()

The spectral component is the same for every pixel: a kappa distribution centered on zero velocity, which has broader wings than a Gaussian. Its width was chosen by hand to be a little wider than the average line profile.

[31]:

velocity = scene_degraded.inputs.velocity.cell_centers(axis_wavelength)
width = 56.25 * u.km / u.s
kappa = 0.2
guess_spectral = (1 + np.square(velocity / width) / kappa) ** (-kappa - 1)
guess_spectral = guess_spectral / guess_spectral.sum()

The guess should also have about the right total signal. To estimate it, backproject the images onto the full grid, which conserves the signal of each channel, and average the totals of the four channels.

[32]:

backprojected = instrument.backproject(images, unit=scene.outputs.unit)
guess_total = backprojected.outputs.sum() / backprojected.shape[axis_channel]

The guess is the product of the three.

[33]:

guess = guess_spectral * guess_spatial * guess_total

Compare the average spectrum of the guess to that of the degraded scene.

[34]:

with astropy.visualization.quantity_support():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(constrained_layout=True)
    na.plt.stairs(
        scene_degraded.inputs.velocity,
        scene_degraded.outputs.mean(axis_xy),
        ax=ax,
        label="degraded scene",
        axis=axis_wavelength,
    )
    na.plt.stairs(
        scene_degraded.inputs.velocity,
        guess.mean(axis_xy),
        ax=ax,
        label="guess",
        axis=axis_wavelength,
    )
    ax.set_xlabel(f"Doppler velocity ({ax.get_xlabel()})")
    ax.set_ylabel(f"average radiance ({ax.get_ylabel()})")
    ax.legend();

Define the MART inverter, a ctis.inverters.MartInverter. intermediate=True saves the solution at every iteration, so we can watch it converge below.

By default, MART stops when the mean \(\chi^2\) improves by less than threshold_convergence from one iteration to the next. With the default threshold this inversion stops after about 12 iterations, while the residuals still show the brightest features of the scene, so we set the threshold to zero and run 25 iterations.

[35]:

mart = ctis.inverters.MartInverter(
    instrument=instrument,
    intermediate=True,
    num_iteration=25,
    threshold_convergence=0,
)

Invert the images, starting from the guess. MART warns when it reaches the iteration limit, which is what we asked for here, so the warning is silenced.

[36]:

%%time
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="Max number of iterations")
    inversion = mart(images, guess=guess, verbose=True)

[41]:

Map the moments of the line profile in each pixel with plot_moments(): the radiance, the median velocity, and the interquartile range (IQR) of the velocity, with the degraded scene above the reconstruction. The median and the IQR mean little where the line is faint, so they are left blank where the signal-to-noise ratio of the reconstructed line profile, snr(), is 4 or less. That ratio is computed from the reconstruction alone, so the same maps can be made for an inversion of observed images, which has no true scene to compare to.

[42]:

ranges = dict(
    range_radiance=[0, 1.5e4] * u.erg / u.s / u.sr / u.cm**2,
    range_median=[-60, 60] * u.km / u.s,
    range_iqr=[0, 100] * u.km / u.s,
)
inversion.plot_moments(
    truth=scene_degraded,
    threshold_snr=4,
    **ranges,
);

Then compare the same moments to those of the degraded scene pixel by pixel, with plot_moments_histogram(). The upper row is the error of each moment against its true value, for the pixels above the same signal-to-noise ratio: the ratio of the reconstructed radiance to the true one, and the reconstructed median and IQR minus the true ones. A dashed line marks no error, and a dotted line marks a reconstruction which is the same in every pixel, and so says nothing about the scene. The lower row is the same error against the signal-to-noise ratio itself, with the threshold marked.

The radiance is recovered with a scatter of about 25%, though the faintest pixels are reconstructed too bright and the brightest ones too faint. The errors of the median lie about halfway between the two lines: the reconstruction recovers about 40% of the Doppler shift of a pixel, with a scatter of about 8 km/s. Those of the IQR lie along the dotted line, so the reconstruction recovers little of the width of the line. In the lower row, the errors narrow as the signal-to-noise ratio rises, and they are widest below the threshold, which is why the maps are left blank there.

[43]:

inversion.plot_moments_histogram(
    truth=scene_degraded,
    threshold_snr=4,
    **ranges,
);

Checking the Residuals#

Finally, image the reconstruction without noise, and subtract the result from the synthetic images. If the inversion had fit the images down to the noise, the residuals would look like noise, with no trace of the Sun. After 25 iterations they are close: the residuals of the brightest features are no larger than the noise there, but they still show some structure.

[44]:

%%time
predictions = instrument.image(solution, noise=False)

CPU times: user 10.4 s, sys: 976 ms, total: 11.4 s
Wall time: 3.64 s

[45]:

residual = images - predictions
